articles.title: investingLive Americas market news wrap: Hawkish Fed worries ebb after PPI
articles.desc: US October PPI +6.5% vs +6.6% expected Fed's Goolsbee: We're not on the way to 2% inflation and we have to deal with that Goldman Sachs: We can explain almost the entire US inflation overshoot by tariffs and the war in Iran Fed's Collins: I would think some additional policy tightening is warranted
articles.content: US October PPI +6.5% vs +6.6% expected Fed's Goolsbee: We're not on the way to 2% inflation and we have to deal with that Goldman Sachs: We can explain almost the entire US inflation overshoot by tariffs and the war in Iran Fed's Collins: I would think some additional policy tightening is warranted soon Fed's Daly: In all likelihood, we need to raise rates Markets: USD leads, AUD lags WTI crude oil up 43-cents to $89.17 US 10-year yields up 3.8 bps to 5.14% S&P 500 down 0.4%, Nasdaq down 0.9% Gold up $4 to $3880 The PPI numbers were something of a respite to the drumbeat of inflation worries as the main numbers were 0.1 pp below estimates. That was generally balanced by non-stop Fed talk on inflation, with Goolsbee saying the recent CPI number was "borderline alarming" and others striking a similar tone. BofA was out with a note to change its Fed call to three consecutive hikes in Dec, Jan and March. All that helped to keep a bid in the dollar, which finisehd at hte best levels of the day. The euro continues to test the Liberation Day lows. In equity markets, the closing levels don't tell the story as the selling was heavily concentrated in AI and chip names. AMD led the re-think with an 8% loss and pre-market gains for Nvidia reversed. The thinking is that the US is going to draw a hard line against China sales and remote use, curbing the market and -- ultimately -- allowing China to build its own chip companies. Outside of that, breadth was positive and there were some bright spots like Meta with a 2.8% gain. Next week features a heavy does of retail earnings so that will be a good check on the consumer. Iran news was generally quiet but there was talk of a strike on US radar facilities in Bahrain. Iran claims it was hit, the US claims the drones were shot down. There was little or nothing on negotiations, so it appears we've reached a standstill and the oil market wasn't overly volatile. Have a great weekend. This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Google Gemini Omni: 5 Things to Know About Google's AI Model
articles.desc: Discover Google Gemini Omni, its multimodal AI capabilities, video generation, conversational editing, character consistency and latest upgrades.
articles.content: Google Gemini Omni: 5 Things to Know About Google's AI Model Google Gemini Omni: 5 Things to Know About Google's AI Model Google is taking AI-powered video creation a step further with Gemini Omni, a multimodal model that combines reasoning with generative media capabilities. It can work with text, images, audio and video to create new visual content. The model also introduces conversational editing, making video creation more accessible. One of Gemini Omni's key features is its ability to combine multiple types of input. Users can provide text prompts, images, video clips and audio references to guide video generation. Instead of starting with a blank screen, creators can use existing material to build a more personalised visual story. Gemini Omni makes video editing more conversational. Users can ask the model to change backgrounds, introduce new objects, modify actions or apply cinematic effects through natural-language prompts. Each instruction builds on the previous edit, reducing the need to recreate an entire video whenever a small change is required. The model is designed to combine visual generation with an understanding of real-world concepts. Google says Gemini Omni can represent physical forces such as gravity, movement and fluid dynamics more realistically. This helps it create scenes that look more coherent, particularly when generating complex actions and cinematic sequences. Maintaining the same character or object across different scenes can be challenging for AI video tools. Gemini Omni aims to improve this by preserving identities, appearances and scene details across successive edits. This can be useful for creators developing short films, advertisements, product videos and other multi-scene content. Google's Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash update, announced in November 2026, extends video generation to up to 15 seconds. It also improves reference consistency, conversational editing, speech generation and lip-sync. These upgrades give creators more flexibility when refining short videos without rebuilding them from the beginning. Gemini Omni Flash is rolling out through Google's Gemini app and Flow, while YouTube Shorts Remix and YouTube Create bring its creative features to short-form video users. Developers can also access the model through Google AI Studio and the Gemini API. U.S. propulsion company Ursa Major has secured a $10.9 million contract option from the Air Force Research Laboratory to continue developing its Draper liquid rocket engine, following two flights of an experimental missile demonstrator powered by the system. The funding will advance Draper, a storable liquid-propellant engine designed for hypersonic applications. The new option follows successful flights of the Affordable Rapid Missile Demonstrator , which uses Draper as its propulsion system. AFRL and Ursa Major first announced a flight demonstration in March 2026, reporting that the vehicle reached supersonic speeds. A follow-on flight took place approximately 45 days later, expanding the demonstrator’s flight envelope and testing the engine’s performance and control during different phases of flight. The flights are an important development milestone, but they should not be confused with a publicly confirmed hypersonic flight. AFRL described the March demonstration as supersonic, while the program’s broader objective is to develop propulsion technology for future high-speed weapons and test vehicles. Draper is designed to combine some of the operational advantages of solid rocket motors with the control offered by liquid propulsion. The engine is also throttleable, meaning its thrust can be adjusted during flight. It can also restart multiple times, according to the company. Draper is also central to the company’s broader hypersonics portfolio. In February 2026, Ursa Major unveiled the HAVOC missile system, describing it as a medium-range hypersonic weapon powered by the Draper engine. The company says HAVOC can throttle and restart during different phases of flight and is designed for potential launches from aircraft, ships, and ground-based systems. Google DeepMind said that the collaboration with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz provides an example of how Google's AI models could support industrial automation. During the proof-of-concept, Apollo 2 robots performed automotive kitting, a process that involves individual components from bulk containers into organized trays in the sequence required for vehicle assembly. The robots retrieved metal automotive brackets from supply bins and placed them into designated sequencing containers. The system also corrected for placement gaps and adapted to changes in its surroundings. "This is what we built Apollo for: useful work alongside people in real industrial settings," said Jeff Cardenas, co-founder and CEO of Apptronik. “Pairing Apollo 2 with Gemini Robotics, we saw the models improve dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training and carry over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off. According to Google's evaluations, the approach improved safe task completion by 33% around obstacles and 43% around nearby people. Google said that Gemini Robotics 2.5 also addresses potential vulnerabilities associated with AI-powered robots. The company introduced ASIMOV-Jailbreak, an benchmark containing hundreds of prompts designed to test whether AI systems can recognize and reject disguised unsafe instructions across different scenarios. articles.title: Committee recommends scaled-back renovations for Westborough community center
articles.content: Committee recommends scaled-back renovations for Westborough community center | Local Government News in Central MA | Community Advocate | communityadvocate.com You have permission to edit this article. WESTBOROUGH – The Municipal Building Committee unanimously approved recommendations Nov. 12 for bidding the community center project with a base package and two alternates, giving the Select Board options as it weighs costs and scope Nov. 16. Based on the estimates presented, the base package totals approximately $14.19 million. Adding the first alternate would bring the project to about $15.62 million, while accepting both alternates would bring it to approximately $17.25 million. The recommendations concern renovations and improvements at 1500 Union St., the former Boston Sports Clubs building intended to house the senior center and veterans center downstairs and recreation facilities upstairs. Exact prices will not be known until competitive bids are received. Town Meeting authorized $8.8 million in borrowing in October 2023 to purchase the 2.58-acre property, and the Select Board voted 5-0 to proceed in March 2024 . The renovation estimates are separate from that acquisition cost. The recommended base bid includes the senior center, estimated at $10.63 million; a new elevator connecting the floors, $932,000; a veterans center, $392,000; an accessible rear entrance, $410,000; building maintenance, $1.059 million; and a new staircase, $271,000, plus listed contingency and soft-cost allowances. The staircase was initially excluded from the architect’s reduced-cost proposal. Members ultimately restored it after discussing the convenience of an internal connection and the disruption of adding stairs later. The first alternate, estimated at $1.43 million, combines two additional program rooms costing $572,000, basic community-room improvements at $500,000 and second-floor improvements at $360,000. Those upstairs changes include relocating administrative offices for better access control and supervision, repairing a room damaged by roof leaks, and improving staff facilities. The second alternate would add approximately $1.64 million beyond the first alternate for a more extensive community-room renovation, including a raised ceiling and new lighting. Members discussed the alternates as sequential choices, meaning accepting the second would require accepting the first. Alternates approved with the contract would be constructed with the main project, while any rejected work would not be included as part of the buildout. The building already contains a basketball court and pool. The cost of reactivating the pool via new pumps and other key equipment is estimated at $803,000 and was excluded from the recommendations. The basic community-room approach would retain existing ceilings and lighting while replacing mixed flooring with vinyl and connecting fire-protection systems. Existing restrooms would remain, with senior center restrooms supplementing them for larger events. The rear entrance has also been simplified to a less expensive ramp design. Including it with the veterans center would allow accessible entry without requiring visitors to pass through the senior center. The all-options estimate totals approximately $19.60 million, compared with $15.35 million for the reduced package—a difference of about $4.25 million. The base-plus-first-alternate estimate was $15.62 million, roughly $3.98 million below the projected total if all improvements to the building in both alternatives were implemented. Town Manager Kristi Williams outlined potential funding using approximately $3.7 million from the Del Webb/Chauncy Lake stabilization fund, free cash matching the $1.6 million Regal settlement and additional free cash covering maintenance. Her draft projections showed borrowing just under $9 million, potentially falling below $6 million after selling the existing senior center property. articles.title: Why Can’t I Stop Over-Drinking on My Own?
articles.desc: Why do intelligent, successful people repeatedly drink to excess, even after experiencing negative consequences? The answer reveals why determination alone is often not enough.
articles.content: Why Can’t I Stop Over-Drinking on My Own? | United States Why Can’t I Stop Over-Drinking on My Own? Why do intelligent, successful people repeatedly drink to excess, even after experiencing negative consequences? The answer reveals why determination alone is often not enough. Repeated heavy drinking can alter brain chemistry, making alcohol use increasingly automatic. Professional treatment and medication can help interrupt persistent, self-destructive drinking patterns. “Why can’t I get my drinking under control? I know I’m drinking too much. I’ve promised myself countless times that I’ll cut back or stop altogether, but sooner or later I end up doing the same thing again. ” I’ve heard some version of this question thousands of times during my 50-plus years of clinical practice as anin other areas of their lives. Roku will stop selling smart home devices and refocus on streaming Yet when it comes to drinking, they repeatedly fail to follow through on their intentions. Why does this happen? And why do some people find it so difficult to change their drinking habits without professional help and/orConsider someone who wakes up after a night of heavy drinking feeling miserable, embarrassed, and absolutely determined never to repeat the experience. Several days later, however, after aworkday or during a social gathering, having a few drinks once again seems innocuous. Yesterday’s determination is displaced by other motivations, some operating outside conscious awareness. Consider the case of a successful businessman who sought my help several months ago after a series of alcohol-related incidents. Two years earlier, he had lost a highly coveted executive position after behaving inappropriately while intoxicated at a company function. Devastated by the experience, he stopped drinking and vowed never again to jeopardize his. Regrettably, several months later, having secured another desirable position, he attended a business dinner followed by several hours of heavy drinking with co-workers at an after-hours club. Despite his earlier resolve and the painful consequences of his previous drinking, he again became severely intoxicated and behaved in ways that once more put his professional standing at risk. How could someone who had already paid such a steep price repeat essentially the same behavior? This is precisely why I titled my first book on addiction treatment, published in 1989,, stress regulation, learning, and self-control. With repeated heavy drinking, the brain can develop a neurochemical relationship with alcohol that makes continued drinking increasingly compelling, even when the person desperately wants to stop. Drinking can begin to operate on something resembling “autopilot,” no longer responding reliably to conscious intentions or rational consideration of its consequences. What initially served a pleasurable or useful purpose becomes a self-perpetuating pattern that continues despite destructive consequences. The behavior has become maladaptive, even self-sabotaging. Over time, drinking becomes associated with particular situations, emotions, and expectations. Arriving home after work, walking into a favorite restaurant, or feeling anxious or upset may automatically trigger the thought that drinking would make everything feel better. These associations become stronger with repetition. Eventually, the urge to drink may arise before the person has consciously considered whether drinking is a good idea and what the potential consequences could be. Another complication arises from the fact that alcohol itself impairs judgment and volitional control. Someone who fully intends to have only two drinks may find that, after consuming them, a third or fourth seems perfectly reasonable. The very substance they are trying to control interferes with their ability to control it. A person’s intention and determination not to overdrink can quickly dissolve in alcohol. Why Do People Miss Drinking Even When They Want to Quit? Alcohol

articles.content: Battalion ship out Karmanov and Vaughan in a pair of Friday deals - North Bay News Battalion ship out Karmanov and Vaughan in a pair of Friday deals 'Today’s trades were not easy but necessary to address some glaring needs we have identified throughout the first quarter of the season' The North Bay Battalion have shipped out top scorer Parker Vaughan and giant defender Alexander Karmanov in a pair of Friday deals, the team announced this morning. The Battalion has acquired centre Dmitry Savin from the Saginaw Spirit in a trade for right winger Parker Vaughan, the Ontario Hockey League club announced Friday. North Bay also sent Saginaw a conditional third-round pick in the 2030 OHL Priority Selection for Savin, a Russian import, while receiving a conditional fifth-round pick in 2030. The pick that the Battalion received was the Spirit’s own, while Saginaw’s new pick originated with the Kingston Frontenacs. To make room for Savin in its three-player import quota, the Battalion moved Moldovan defenceman Alexander Karmanov to the Windsor Spitfires for a sixth-round choice in 2030. “Today’s trades were not easy but necessary to address some glaring needs we have identified throughout the first quarter of the season,” said Adam Dennis, Battalion director of hockey operations. “I want to thank both Parker and Alex for their dedication and professionalism throughout their time here. They both will be missed, and we wish them nothing but the best with their new clubs.” Vaughan leads the Battalion in points with 21. He went undrafted in the 2026 NHL Entry Draft but was invited to the Toronto Maple Leafs training camp. In the meantime, Karmanov, the biggest drafted player in NHL history, was selected in the 7th round by the San Jose Sharks. Karmanov had only dressed for 11 of the Battalion's first 20 games to start the season. The Battalion signed Karmanov on Nov. 26, 2025, after securing his rights from the Brantford Titans of the Greater Ontario Hockey League. Karmanov, who measures seven feet and 272 pounds, is the tallest player in CHL history. A native of Chisinau, the capital of Moldova, who turned 18 on March 22, he is the world’s tallest active registered hockey player. A left shot who measures six-foot-three and 190 pounds, he turned 17 on April 14. Savin is a native of the Siberian centre of Novosibirsk, the third-largest city in Russia. The Spirit praised him for being a talented two-way centre when they drafted him in the summer, but the domino effect coming down from the National Hockey League forced the U.S. based OHL team to look at options for Savin. "We admire the attention to detail in all aspects of his game, especially given how young he is. He’ll fit right in with the rest of our skilled young players, and we’re so happy to be able to sign him," said Dave Drinkhill, Spirit general manager, after the Import Draft last July. Savin had four goals and seven assists for 11 points in 19 games with Saginaw. articles.title: LANL Moves High Performance Computing to Open-Source, Scalable Systems Management
articles.content: HPCwire - Since 1987 – Covering the Fastest Computers in the World and the People Who Run Them Penguin Solutions Introduces CXL-Enabled DDR4 Module for AI Data Centers Marvell Scales Connectivity to Address AI Infrastructure’s Next Bottleneck at SC26 BSC at SC26: From RISC-V to Quantum Computing HPE Introduces Hybrid HPC Storage and Rack Management Controller Staera Semiconductor Emerges from Stealth with $4.6M to Break AI’s Data Bottleneck QuiX Quantum Secures PhotonDelta Funding for Photonic Quantum Computing Delta Electronics Showcases AI Data Center Cooling Solutions at SC26 Quantum Elements’ Constellation Platform Leveraged by Rigetti Florida Atlantic University Receives $3M to Build Statewide Quantum-Ready Workforce LANL Moves High Performance Computing to Open-Source, Scalable Systems Management Majority of Los Alamos computing now runs on OpenCHAMI framework reached a milestone recently with the completion of its move of most production computing to Open, Composable, Heterogenous, Adaptable, Management Infrastructure (OpenCHAMI). The OpenCHAMI framework offers modern systems-management methods with built-in flexibility for sites like Los Alamos to deploy their preferred tools. In total, seven Los Alamos production clusters totaling more than 11,000 compute nodes now run on OpenCHAMI. Launched in 2023, the open community collaboration included as founding members Los Alamos, the National Energy Research Scientific Computing (NERSC) Center at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the Swiss National Supercomputing Center (CSCS), HPE and the University of Bristol; Dell joined the collaboration in 2024. The collaboration came together under an open governance model to build a framework that was faster, simpler and more flexible than a traditional system and that sites could control at scales to fit their needs. The cloud-native technology helps institutions leverage build-and-configure tools and actively manage operations and change. “Building the framework and transitioning the Lab’s computing to the system demonstrates the value of OpenCHAMI for large-scale computing environments running hardware and software from multiple vendors,” said Markus Berndt, High Performance Computing division leader at Los Alamos. “With the framework in place at our site, we’ve already seen reduced downtime for upgrades, meaning we can spend more time with our resources focused on mission-relevant activities.” An Adaptation for Challenging Applications The high-performance computing (HPC) teams at Los Alamos and partnering institutions recognized the challenges of running sophisticated applications such as complex simulations, data analytics, AI applications and heterogenous workflows at scale in hybrid computing environments. Typically, computing centers tended toward installing, configuring systems, then resisting changes or embarking on upgrades complicated by legacy tools inherent in the infrastructure. Two of the biggest HPC vendors in the United States, HPE and Dell, have partnered on the effort. The open-source basis of OpenCHAMI means that the framework can be deployed with both those ecosystems. OpenCHAMI also centers innovation and customization, including the deployment of site-appropriate micro-services, heterogeneous orchestration, self-discovery and healing, adaptability and composability — all tools that help accommodate different needs without sacrificing performance. Importantly, the inherent flexibility of the OpenCHAMI framework benefits the mission-supporting modeling and simulation and artificial intelligence computing systems deployed at the Laboratory. OpenCHAMI provides the capability to perform tasks that are key to running AI systems; for instance, quickly changing over an operating system running on subset of nodes. “HPE became a founding member of the OpenCHAMI project to advance secure, scalable and modern system management for high-performance computing and drive our commitment to open standards,” said Shawn T. articles.title: Review: Abarth 600e Competizione
articles.desc: The Abarth 600e has been reborn with two new trim levels
articles.content: The Abarth 600e has been reborn with two new trim levels At the beginning of 2026, Abarth introduced two new trims for its sporty electric 600e, replacing the original launch editions. The 600e became Turismo, while Scorpionissima was renamed Competizione. The change was necessary because Scorpionissima is traditionally reserved for Abarth launch models. These are limited to 1,949 examples, paying tribute to the year the firm was founded in , on March 31, 1949. Once that initial batch sells out, a new name is chosen. I first drove the Scorpionissima in summer 2025 and loved it, so I was pleased to get reacquainted with the car in its new Competizione guise. In essence, it is the same machine, powered by a 54kWh battery and offering an official range of 207 miles. Marketed as being “born on the track, enhanced for the road”, it is the result of a joint project between Abarth and Stellantis Motorsport engineers. With a blistering 0-62mph time of under six seconds and a top speed of 124mph, it is the fastest Abarth ever made. Driving the 600e is enormous fun. It corners confidently and offers three driving modes: Turismo, Scorpion Street and Scorpion Track, delivering 195bhp, 224bhp and 276bhp respectively. Regenerative braking also varies according to the mode selected. As you might expect with that much power available, range is not its strongest point. The Competizione’s claimed 207 miles can be difficult to achieve, particularly if you spend much of your time in Scorpion Track. Drive enthusiastically, or in extreme weather, and the figure will fall further. Charging is swift, with a 20 to 80 per cent top-up taking around 30 minutes using a rapid charger. There’s plenty of flexibility to help the driver find a comfortable seating position, while the passenger seat also offers four-way movement. Our test car came in eye-catching Acid Green with a black roof. It will not be to everyone’s taste, but I am a real fan. Equipment is generous, including wireless Apple CarPlay, adaptive cruise control, satellite navigation through the 10.25-inch infotainment screen and automatic climate control. A wireless charging pad, USB ports for rear passengers, front, rear and side parking sensors, and a reversing camera add to the specification. Rear-seat space is limited, although adequate for occasional use. Boot capacity is 360 litres, and the adjustable floor makes lifting heavier items easier when set at its highest position. There is also a hands-free tailgate. Folding the rear seats in a 60:40 split increases capacity to 1,231 litres. Cabin storage is decent, too, with several useful places to stow smaller items. One large compartment is covered by an unusual soft, magnetic folding lid, complete with “Mind The Scorpion” stitching on the front. The 600e remains a distinctive, entertaining electric hot hatch, with performance that puts a smile on your face. Just do not expect to get close to its official range if you make full use of its considerable pace. Price: £37,995 with government’s £1,500 grant) Iconic Media Group Ltd. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Friday the 13th origins: 10 theories, from the Knights Templar to a 1907 novel
articles.desc: Why Friday the 13th is unlucky has no proven answer, but these 10 origin theories trace the superstition from the Knights Templar and Norse myth to a 1907 novel
articles.content: Why Friday the 13th is unlucky: 10 theories on its origin Friday the 13th origins: 10 theories, from the Knights Templar to a 1907 novel Why Friday the 13th is unlucky has no proven answer, but these 10 origin theories trace the superstition from the Knights Templar and Norse myth to a 1907 novel Friday the 13th is really two superstitions stacked on one date. One is an old unease about the number 13, known as triskaidekaphobia. The other is a long-standing sense that Friday is a bad day to begin anything important. Each half has roots that reach back centuries. Their pairing into a single feared date appears to be more recent than either piece on its own. That split matters for anyone asking why Friday the 13th is unlucky. There is no single origin story, and no document marks the moment the belief began. What exists instead is a set of proposed explanations. Some account for the number. Some account for the weekday. A few try to explain the combination itself. Those explanations come from different traditions. Christian tradition supplies two of them, one tied to a dinner table and one tied to the day of the week. Norse mythology offers a story about an unwelcome guest at a banquet of the gods. The English name for Friday traces back to a Germanic goddess. Medieval English literature shows that Friday already carried a dark reputation in the late 1300s. Maritime lore adds the sailor's reluctance to leave port on a Friday. Other theories point to specific moments in history. A French king ordered the arrest of members of the Knights Templar across France on a Friday the 13th in 1307. An Italian opera composer died on one in 1868. A Boston financier published a novel in 1907 that put the date at the center of a Wall Street plot. None of these theories is proven. Some rest on well-documented dates but offer weak evidence of any link to the superstition. Others are interpretations of why a number or a day might feel unsettling. A few circulate mainly through popular retellings. The 10 explanations below are a selection of proposed origins, not a complete or ranked list. The fear of the date itself has its own name: paraskevidekatriaphobia. The word combines Greek roots for Friday, the number 13 and fear. Each slide below examines one theory on its own terms. It sets out what is documented, what is assumed and where the story drifts into legend. Knights Templar arrests on Friday, October 13, 1307 King Philip IV of France ordered the arrest of Knights Templar members across France on Friday, October 13, 1307. Popular retellings name that day as the start of the Friday the 13th superstition. No firm medieval evidence ties the two together. The Knights Templar began in Jerusalem around 1120 as a small group of knights pledged to protect Christian pilgrims traveling to the Holy Land. The Catholic Church gave the order formal backing at the Council of Troyes in 1129. Over the next two centuries, it grew into a wealthy international organization with property across Europe. Much of that wealth came from donations of land and money. The order also held and moved funds for pilgrims and rulers, a service that resembled early banking. By the start of the 14th century, the Templars controlled significant assets in France. Philip IV, sometimes called Philip the Fair, owed the order money. His officers carried out the arrests as a coordinated operation on a single day. The Templars faced charges of heresy, including denying Christ and spitting on the cross. Many confessed under torture. Several later withdrew those confessions. Pope Clement V dissolved the order in 1312. Jacques de Molay, its last grand master, was burned at the stake in Paris in 1314. The date of the arrests is well documented. The leap from that date to a lasting fear of Friday the 13th is where the story weakens. Records from the period describe the arrests. None of them presents the day itself as cursed or treats the date as a warning to later generations. The connection

articles.title: CRISPR Therapy For Sickle Cell Disease Faces FDA Scrutiny Amid Safety Concerns - BW Healthcare World
articles.desc: CRISPR–Cas9 genome editing system-based therapy is on the verge of gaining approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). On Wednesday, external advisers to the FDA will meet to deliberate on the DNA-altering therapy designed to combat sickle-cell disease. Sickle cell is a genetic conditio
articles.content: CRISPR–Cas9 genome editing system-based therapy is on the verge of gaining approval from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). On Wednesday, external advisers to the FDA will meet to deliberate on the DNA-altering therapy designed to combat sickle-cell disease. Sickle cell is a genetic condition that can lead to malformed blood cells and excruciating pain in patients. The discussions during this meeting are expected to be primarily focused on the safety data submitted by the developers of the treatment, Vertex Pharmaceuticals based in Boston, Massachusetts, and CRISPR Therapeutics in Zug, Switzerland. Mark Walters, a paediatrician at the University of California, San Francisco, who has been part of a steering committee advising the two companies on the clinical development of the treatment, known as exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel), emphasised the paramount importance of safety. He noted that safety data remains somewhat limited and that this crucial aspect could significantly influence the decision-making process. Sickle-cell disease results from abnormal forms of haemoglobin, the protein responsible for transporting oxygen in red blood cells. The altered haemoglobin causes blood cells to become misshapen and adhesive, leading to the clumping of cells and potential blockages in blood vessels. This deprivation of oxygen can cause long-term damage and severe episodes of pain referred to as vaso-occlusive crises. Exa-cel aims to mitigate these issues by reactivating the production of another form of haemoglobin typically present only in developing fetuses. The BCL11A gene typically shuts down the production of fetal haemoglobin shortly after birth. Exa-cel effectively disables BCL11A, enabling the resumption of fetal haemoglobin production. This provides a source of normal haemoglobin, alleviating the effects of the abnormal form. In their clinical trial, Vertex and CRISPR Therapeutics reported that, nine months after treatment, 39 out of 40 participants had not experienced a single vaso-occlusive crisis. Prior to treatment, they had, on average, suffered from around four crises each year. The process involves collecting blood-producing stem cells from individuals with sickle-cell disease, followed by treatment with a genome editor. This editor includes the Cas9 enzyme, which cuts DNA, and a guiding molecule directing the enzyme to the specific stretch of DNA within the BCL11A gene. Cas9 cuts both DNA strands at that region, and the cell's natural DNA-repair mechanisms mend the strands. However, these repairs are prone to errors, often introducing mutations in the DNA sequence that disable BCL11A and allow fetal haemoglobin production to resume. One critical concern with CRISPR–Cas9 therapies is that Cas9 can sometimes mistakenly cut DNA at other regions in the genome that resemble its target. Repairs to this 'off-target' DNA can lead to unwanted mutations. The FDA has identified this as a crucial issue in the case of exa-cel and is expected to discuss it extensively during the upcoming meeting. The FDA has raised concerns about the assays used by Vertex and CRISPR Therapeutics to assess exa-cel's risk of causing off-target changes. One assay involved searching a genome database for regions similar to exa-cel's CRISPR–Cas9 target site that could be mistakenly cleaved by the Cas9 enzyme. The genetic diversity of populations predominantly affected by sickle-cell disease, notably people of African descent, was not adequately represented in these genome searches, according to the FDA. This implies that there may be genetic sequences in these populations that could be targeted by Cas9 but were missed during the analysis. Additionally, the FDA has expressed unease that the companies' assays for detecting off-target effects in live cells did not include a sufficient number of cells from people with sickle-cell disease. One significant concern, beyond off-target edits, is that two participants in a clinical trial involving a different gene-altering therapy for sickle-cell disease developed blood cancers afterwards. This trial, conducted by Bluebird Bio in Cambridge, Massachusetts, used a virus to deliver non-sickled haemoglobin into blood stem cells. Subsequent investigations determined that the cancers were not caused by the virus, raising speculation that similar cases might occur with other therapies like exa-cel, which modify blood stem cells and reinfuse them. Some studies suggest that individuals with sickle-cell disease may be more susceptible to malignant blood cancers. If precancerous cells were reintroduced, the therapy might inadvertently support their growth into cancerous cells. In response to these concerns, Vertex and CRISPR Therapeutics have proposed a 15-year follow-up of trial participants to monitor the potential long-term impacts of the treatment. Advocates stress the importance of physicians informing patients about the associated risks, given the uncertainties surrounding these therapies.

articles.title: How the brain decides which moments to remember – and which to forget
articles.desc: Scientists have mapped how extreme moments trigger a biological chain reaction that locks memories into place
articles.content: How the brain decides which moments to remember – and which to forget | The Independent Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. have uncovered how extreme or frightening moments trigger a rapid biological chain reaction in the while letting everyday routines fade away. Researchers at the University of Utah found that a small, almond-shaped structure deep inside the brain – known as the – acts as a vital gatekeeper during moments of sudden shock, danger, or excitement. , brings together decades of laboratory research and human clinical trials to map how the brain filters human experience. Normally, the brain discards the vast majority of mundane daily routines – such as a routine trip to the shops – to avoid becoming overwhelmed by trivial details. But when something intense or deeply emotional happens, the amygdala switches on and prompts neighbouring brain regions to preserve the moment for long-term recall. The chain reaction begins the moment a person encounters a sudden threat or intense surprise. Adrenal glands sitting atop the kidneys release adrenaline into the bloodstream, stimulating a region in the brainstem. That brainstem region then delivers a chemical messenger called norepinephrine directly into the amygdala. Once activated, the amygdala does not act as a storage vault itself. Instead, it functions as an internal alert hub that directs the hippocampus—a seahorse-shaped structure essential for memory formation and retrieval—to record sensory details as an event unfolds. By sending electrical signals and protein-triggering messages to the hippocampus, the amygdala strengthens connections between brain cells. This prompts the hippocampus to gather sights, sounds, smells, and physical sensations from separate neural hubs, including the visual, auditory, and olfactory cortices, binding them together for later recall. To test this circuit directly in humans, researchers studied epilepsy patients who already had electrodes surgically implanted in their brains for medical monitoring. During trials, participants were shown a series of images on a computer screen before doctors delivered a tiny, imperceptible electrical pulse directly to the amygdala. When tested the following day, patients were significantly better at recognising the pictures paired with the electrical stimulation than those viewed without it. By contrast, routine physical habits – such as tying shoelaces or kicking a ball – bypass this emotional alert system entirely, relying instead on a brain region called the striatum. The researchers stressed that human recall does not work like replaying an unedited film. When retrieving a past event, the brain stitches stored sensory fragments back together, occasionally filling in missing gaps based on surrounding context. Mapping how this circuit operates marks a major step forward in understanding human memory, opening the door to targeted therapies for severe memory loss, dementia, and trauma-related conditions. articles.title: A new phage in the fight against antibiotic resistance
articles.desc: A new discovery moves us closer to enlisting bacteria‑killing viruses in the fight against antibiotic resistance, Manuela Fuchs, Leah Smith and Natalie Kyte write.
articles.content: A new phage in the fight against antibiotic resistance With their spindly legs and geometric heads, they look more like miniature spacecraft than anything living on Earth. But bacteriophages, or simply phages, are among the most abundant biological entities on the planet. These microscopic agents are viruses that can infect and kill bacteria, offering an intriguing alternative to antibiotics at a time when drug-resistant infections are threatening global health. However, despite decades of research, scientists still know surprisingly little about how most phages work. Many of their genes have functions that remain a mystery, limiting their potential in medicine and elsewhere. Now, our new research offers a way to investigate them in greater detail. We’ve developed a method to pinpoint which genes phages need to function, and to insert new genetic material into their genomes within days. This might eventually help researchers engineer phages that are better at attacking harmful bacteria — opening up possibilities for treating infections that conventional antibiotics struggle against. Long before antibiotics became the standard treatment for bacterial infections, doctors were using phages to fight them. Phages were first used in this way a century ago. But with the arrival of antibiotics, inconsistent results from early phage treatments and the onset of the Cold War, their medical use declined in Western countries. In his 1945 Nobel Prize lecture, Alexander Fleming, who discovered penicillin, warned that bacteria could develop resistance to antibiotics. His warning proved prescient. As new antibiotics were developed, resistant bacteria emerged, helped by the overuse and misuse of these drugs. Today, antibiotic resistance is projected to contribute to more than 8 million deaths annually by 2050, prompting renewed interest in phage-based treatments. Despite their growing use in medicine and agriculture, much of what we know about phages comes from a small number of well-studied examples. Their vast diversity, and the functions of many of their genes, remain largely unexplored. Like humans, phages have genomes containing genes that carry instructions for making proteins. These proteins determine how the viruses function, including how they infect bacteria and reproduce. To investigate phage gene function, scientists need tools that can boost our understanding and turn new knowledge into practical applications. Current methods for studying and modifying phages can be time-consuming, work only with certain bacteria, or require detailed knowledge of the phage’s genome. We wanted to overcome these limitations by developing a method that could work across different phages and their bacterial hosts. To do this, we harnessed transposons — mobile pieces of DNA that insert themselves into random positions in a genome and disrupt gene function. Our approach, called Phage Tn-seq (transposon sequencing), combines these insertions with DNA sequencing, allowing us to pinpoint where mutations occur and how they affect the phage. Since the late 2000s, similar techniques have helped scientists understand bacterial gene function. Typically, transposons carry an antibiotic resistance gene, allowing bacteria that receive them to survive antibiotic treatment. But this doesn’t work directly with phages, which aren’t affected by antibiotics. Instead, we exploited what has been described as a molecular “arms race” between bacteria and the phages that infect them. Bacteria have evolved CRISPR-Cas immune systems, which recognise and cut up invading viral DNA, to defend themselves against phages. In turn, some phages have developed anti-CRISPR proteins that overcome these defences. We used one of these proteins, carried on the transposon, instead of an antibiotic resistance gene. articles.title: How Nara Lokesh plans to connect college students and startups with India's space economy
articles.desc: Andhra Pradesh to build unique space economy ecosystem, says minister Lokesh
articles.content: Nara Lokesh outlines space sector opportunities for students How Nara Lokesh plans to connect college students and startups with India's space economy At the CII Partnership Summit 2026, the Andhra Pradesh minister emphasised horizontal and vertical integration to bring academia, component manufacturers, and private space firms into a single industrial ecosystem Andhra Pradesh to build unique space economy ecosystem, says minister Lokesh Andhra Pradesh Education and IT Minister Nara Lokesh on Friday expressed confidence that Andhra Pradesh, unlike other states, will build a unique space economy ecosystem. Speaking at a session on India's New Space Economy on the second day of the CII Partnership Summit 2026 in Visakhapatnam, Lokesh said the space economy was at the beginning of an exciting phase, with enormous opportunities yet to be explored. The Minister said Andhra Pradesh had created a strong sense of excitement around the space economy and was positioning itself differently from other states. He emphasised that a thriving industrial ecosystem could not be developed merely through incentives or freebies, but required collective efforts and collaboration among all stakeholders. He highlighting the growing opportunities for startups, entrepreneurs and research institutions. He stressed the importance of bringing together thought leaders, entrepreneurs and academia to create a sustainable and vibrant space industry ecosystem. According to him, close collaboration among these groups would be essential to identify opportunities, encourage innovation and translate emerging ideas into successful ventures. Expressing confidence in the state's vision, Lokesh said that Andhra Pradesh was committed to turning its ambitions into reality. The Minister added that Andhra Pradesh would work towards building a distinctive and thriving ecosystem for the space economy through collective leadership, entrepreneurship and academic collaboration. Addressing college students on the emerging opportunities in the space economy, Lokesh noted how state governments can contribute to a sector largely governed by the Central government. He said Andhra Pradesh is adopting a systematic approach to developing sector-specific ecosystems by identifying key industries, mapping all stakeholders and attracting investments and companies to the state. He emphasised the need for strong vertical and horizontal integration to build a comprehensive space industry ecosystem. Vertical integration involves attracting sub-component manufacturers, suppliers and vendors who support major space companies such as Skyroot in developing and launching their rockets. Lokesh said that a significant number of these supporting companies are Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), which play a crucial role in strengthening the supply chain. Citing an example, he mentioned meeting an MSME exhibitor that had manufactured a shield for a rocket. Explaining horizontal integration, Lokesh said it involves bringing academia and industry together by revamping academic curricula, encouraging research and strengthening testing and certification facilities through Centres of Excellence. He highlighted the collaboration with IIT Tirupati to establish a Centre of Excellence in the energy sector, particularly in view of the growing cluster of ingot, solar wafer and solar cell manufacturing companies in the region. Lokesh also stressed the need for a dedicated national policy to develop an integrated space industry ecosystem and said state governments should proactively identify and attract companies such as Skyroot. He called for a systematic approach to identifying the entire value chain, including component manufacturers, suppliers and vendors, and bringing them together within a common industrial ecosystem.
